content: Communities that are already vulnerable often face a higher risk of diseases, particularly in areas prone to disasters. Limited access to safe drinking water and inadequate water supplies for basic hygiene significantly impact children's health. In urban areas of many developing countries, the use of polluting household fuels is still widespread. This not only exacerbates the already high levels of urban air pollution but also contributes significantly to ambient air pollution. Traditionally, child health improvement programs have been implemented as isolated, vertical initiatives, each with its own staff, budget, and resources. Transitioning from these siloed approaches to more integrated and collaborative efforts can reduce costs and enhance the impact of interventions. Such efforts should involve not only the health sector but also foster stronger connections with other sectors. Understanding risks, local contexts, and identifying realistic points of convergence between interventions is essential for ensuring quality and integrity in implementation. Examples of integrated approaches include integrated logistics, integrated service delivery, and integrated outreach. Efforts to reduce childhood deaths from pneumonia and diarrhea have demonstrated the benefits of integrated intervention delivery. For instance, in Malawi, combining hygiene kit distribution with antenatal care (ANC) led to a nearly 30-fold increase in household water treatment practices three years after the intervention. It also resulted in a 15% increase in health facility deliveries and postnatal checkups, both indicators of improved maternal and child health. Sanitation and household water treatment are critical focus areas for cross-sectoral collaboration. In Mali, the Ministry of Health (MoH) developed a strategic plan (2011–2015) targeting diarrheal disease prevention through hygiene promotion. This plan outlined responsibilities across various stakeholders and ministries, with the MoH overseeing integrated management of childhood illnesses (IMCI), which includes water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) messaging. Similarly, Ethiopia has a memorandum of understanding between the MoH, Ministry of Water and Energy, and Ministry of Education to coordinate WASH services, particularly sanitation and water quality surveillance. Over 35,000 health extension workers (HEWs) are involved in these efforts, alongside local leaders and communities. In Western Kenya, integrating household water treatment and handwashing education with maternal and child health services has shown promising results. Pregnant women received hygiene kits, nutrition kits, and delivery kits during ANC visits, which significantly increased attendance rates, health facility deliveries, and postnatal checkups. This approach also improved water treatment practices and handwashing techniques. The initiative involved national and international partners, including the Kenyan Ministry of Public Health, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control, and the World Health Organization (WHO). National governments must lead the development, implementation, and financing of strategies to reduce pneumonia and diarrhea morbidity and mortality. These efforts should align with existing national child health or survival strategies. Key actions include developing clear country-level strategies, generating political will, prioritizing interventions, and ensuring resources are allocated effectively. Advocacy efforts should target policymakers, parliamentarians, and other stakeholders to secure commitments to reducing child deaths from these diseases. A situation analysis should be conducted to review current intervention coverage, identify barriers to scaling up, and propose solutions. This analysis should also address policy issues, such as empowering community health workers (CHWs) to manage pneumonia with antibiotics and use zinc in diarrhea treatment. Countries should prioritize interventions with the strongest evidence for reducing child mortality, such as vaccination, case management, breastfeeding, and access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene facilities. Integrated approaches, such as IMCI, have proven effective in addressing multiple health challenges. Lessons learned from large-scale outbreaks, such as cholera, can be applied to pneumonia and diarrhea control. National working groups should track progress using key indicators incorporated into district and national surveillance systems. Strengthening data collection and ensuring accountability for action are critical for achieving sustained improvements in child health outcomes.
